markdownRemark.html:
At the end of the HSL and HSV article I had a complaint: HSL’s “L” says pure yellow and pure blue are equally light, and anyone can see they aren’t. So what would an honest lightness look like? The answer is a color system called Lab, and this is what I learned about it.

Here is what I wanted to know:

  • What is Lab, and why does it have an “L*” with a star?
  • What do a* and b* mean?
  • Can I measure the difference between two colors with a number?
  • Where does Lab fall short?

The color series: 1. What an RGB number actually means · 2. Where the horseshoe comes from · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see (you are here) · 5. Why gradients go muddy

Disclaimer: This is the article where I trust Claude’s math least, because Lab has lots of constants, so I recomputed every number in the text. The history is Claude’s explanation and I have only secondary sources for it. I’m learning in public, and I’d rather be corrected than be confidently wrong, so if your Lab numbers differ from mine, tell me in the comments.

Key takeaways:

  • Lab is a coordinate system where distance matches perceived difference (roughly). Its L* is a real lightness, which HSL’s L never was.
  • L* is about the cube root of luminance. An 18% gray sits at L* 49.5, about halfway up, which is also how it looks.
  • a* and b* are opponent axes: green to red and blue to yellow, with gray in the middle at every lightness.
  • A distance in Lab is a color difference you can see: ΔE. LCh turns Lab into an honest hue wheel.
  • Lab has flaws: blues drift toward purple, and big distances are less trustworthy. Oklab fixes much of it.

What is Lab, then?

Lab (properly CIELAB) is a coordinate system the CIE standardized in 1976 for one purpose: a distance in the numbers should match a difference you can see. It fixes the two things I complained about earlier: HSL’s lightness that knows nothing about the eye, and the stretched greens on the chart from Where the horseshoe comes from.

It isn’t a screen color space and it has no gamut of its own. It is a set of device-independent coordinates, and every color a person can see has a place in it. To get a hex color into Lab you go through the steps from What an RGB number actually means and Where the horseshoe comes from:

hex → undo the transfer curve → linear RGB → 3×3 matrix → XYZ → Lab

The transfer curve and the matrix come from the color space, and XYZ is where the horseshoe’s chart comes from. The last step is where the design decisions are. There are two.

Decision 1: a cube root for lightness

The formulas, with Y, X and Z the color’s XYZ values and Yn, Xn, Zn those of the white (D65):

L* = 116 · f(Y / Yn) − 16

a* = 500 · [f(X / Xn) − f(Y / Yn)]

b* = 200 · [f(Y / Yn) − f(Z / Zn)]

f(t) is, for most colors, just a cube root: f(t) = t^(1/3). The reason is that perceived lightness follows roughly the cube root of luminance, a finding that goes back to work on the Munsell color system (I have only secondary sources for that, so treat the history as Claude’s explanation). Here is the curve, with a straight line for comparison:

Interactive illustration (lightness-curve). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

A concrete number: an 18% gray, the classic “middle gray” of photography, gives L* = 116 × 0.18^(1/3) − 16 = 49.5. An 18% gray really does look like it’s halfway between black and white, and on this scale it lands halfway.

For nerds: the short straight piece in f(t)

Claude explained this to me. The definition is on Wikipedia.

Written out, the function is

  • f(t) = t^(1/3) if t > ε
  • f(t) = (κ·t + 16) / 116 otherwise

with ε = 216/24389 (about 0.008856) and κ = 24389/27 (about 903.3). A cube root is extremely steep at zero, so the CIE swaps in a straight line for the very darkest colors, just as the sRGB curve does near black. It matches the cube root in value and slope where they meet.

Now the payoff for the HSL “lies”. Twelve colors, all with the same HSL saturation and lightness (S 100%, L 50%), and the L* each one really has:

Interactive illustration (hsl-vs-lab-lightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Yellow is at L* 97 and blue at L* 32. The same “L 50%” in HSL covers everything from 32 to 97. And the almost-black #1A0000 that HSL called 100% saturated has an L* of 2: it is simply very dark. Flip the switch to see each color as the gray with the same L*, and you see how uneven “50%” was.

Decision 2: opponent channels

The other two coordinates copy how the eye works. The retina doesn’t pass the three cone signals straight to the brain; it recombines them into opponent channels: light–dark, red–green and yellow–blue. (This is Claude’s explanation, not something I looked up.) That is why “reddish yellow” (orange) is easy to imagine and “reddish green” isn’t: each opponent pair sits at the two ends of a single channel.

Lab does the same:

  • a*: negative is green, positive is red.
  • b*: negative is blue, positive is yellow.
  • a* = b* = 0 is gray, at any L*.

The 500 and 200 in the formulas just scale the axes so equal steps look roughly equal.

Fix a lightness and you get a flat picture: a* across, b* up, gray in the middle. Here is that slice. The hatched part is colors sRGB can’t show at that lightness, and the ring marks the most colorful color sRGB does have there. Slide the lightness:

Interactive illustration (lab-plane). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

At L* 32 the most colorful sRGB color is a blue (chroma 131), at L* 75 a green, and at L* 97 a yellow (chroma 96). Close to black and close to white there is almost nothing left, which is why a color pushed very dark or very light has to lose its color: there is no room for it.

My dark teal #33505C (from the exposure and HSL articles), comes out as L* 32.3, a* −7.2, b* −10.4: fairly dark, a little green, quite a bit blue.

Distance means something now

Because the axes are meant to be even, you can measure the difference between two colors as a plain straight-line distance:

ΔE = √(ΔL*² + Δa*² + Δb*²)

A worked example. #33505C and #365360 differ by 3 or 4 in each channel, which is invisible to me. Their ΔE is 1.4. For the original formula (called CIE76), a ΔE of about 2.3 is often quoted as one “just noticeable difference”, although the design target was 1 and other studies say other things (Wikipedia’s color difference article has the history). Compare that with #FFFF00 against #0000FF: a ΔE of 235. In RGB or on the xy chart, the same size of numerical step can be invisible in one place and huge in another. That is the point of Lab.

LCh: the honest cylinder

Lab can be turned into the same cylinder idea as HSL, with the axes made honest:

C = √(a*² + b*²) (chroma, the distance from gray)

h = atan2(b*, a*) (the hue angle)

The teal comes out at C = 12.7 and h = 235°. In HSL the same color had a hue of 198°. Same color, two different hue wheels, two different numbers. (They also run through the colors in different places: yellow is at 60° in HSL, and at about 103° in LCh.)

A small thing I want to remember for my own editing: when I split a picture into “green and teal things” and “warm skin tones” by hue, a cut made on the LCh wheel follows what I see better than a cut made on the HSL wheel. As real examples, a teal-green like #1F8A70 sits at an LCh hue of about 171°, while skin tones like #C68642, #E0AC69 and #8D5524 sit around 63° to 75°.

Where Lab falls short

  • Blue drift. Lab predicts hue badly for blues: along a line of constant hue, saturated blues drift toward purple as the chroma changes. This is its best-known flaw.
  • Big distances are less trustworthy than small ones. Newer distance formulas such as CIEDE2000 were built to correct for this.
  • Oklab. In 2020 Björn Ottosson published Oklab, which keeps Lab’s structure (L, a, b) but is fitted to better appearance data and fixes much of the blue problem. CSS has adopted it.
  • Which white. The Lab above uses the D65 white that sRGB uses. CSS’s lab() is defined with a D50 white (the print industry’s), so the same hex color gets slightly different Lab numbers in a browser. Same idea, a slightly different white.

If you want to explore it yourself, the color tools page has a Lab explorer: pick any point on the slice and it tells you the color, the chroma and the hue, and whether sRGB can show it.

What I took away

Lab is the attempt to make the numbers match the eye. L* gives an honest lightness (about a cube root of luminance), a* and b* are opponent axes, and distances in the space are color differences you can see. That makes it the right tool for comparing colors, masking by hue and building smooth ramps, and the wrong one for anything about physics.

Which brings me to the question that started all of this for me. When a program draws a gradient between two colors, which space does it do the math in? It turns out the answer changes the middle of the gradient completely. That is Why gradients go muddy.

Did I get something wrong, or do you use Lab differently? The comments are open.

frontmatter.title: Lab: numbers that match what you see
frontmatter.description: HSL's lightness is fake, so what would an honest one look like? What Lab is, why L* is about a cube root, what ΔE measures, and where Lab goes wrong.
